newsitem.title: UK: Six candidates vie for UK Conservative leadership.
newsitem.headline: Six candidates vie for UK Conservative leadership.

text.p: The fight to lead Britain's defeated Conservative Party turned into a six-horse race on Wednesday when former Welsh secretary William Hague and ex-health secretary Stephen Dorrell put themselves forward.
"I am standing as someone who wants to see the future rebuilt," Dorrell told the BBC.
He said he wanted "to rethink the policy position of the Conservative Party so we address the concerns of the voters directly".
Hague also used the BBC to confirm that he would be standing.
"I think the Conservative Party needs a fresh start after a very heavy election defeat and I think I am best placed to provide it."

So far, pro-European former finance minister Kenneth Clarke, right-wing former social security secretary Peter Lilley, former interior minister Michael Howard and arch-anti-European John Redwood have put themselves forward to succeed John Major.
Major announced he was stepping down last Friday, the morning after Tony Blair's Labour Party dealt the Conservatives their worst election defeat since 1832.

Hague, aged just 36, has become the bookmakers' favourite since former deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine threw the race wide open by deciding he would not stand after he was admitted to hospital at the weekend due to a heart scare.
Hague had reached agreement to stand as deputy leader to Howard, but later pulled out of the deal, an action which has led to charges of indecision.
Hague rejected this and said people would discover that he knew exactly what he had to do.
"I want to reaffirm the basic values of the Conservative Party," Hague said. "The Conservative Party has got to recover its self belief and its will to win."
"It has to be ready to learn from the Labour Party in its methods of communication."
Hague confirmed that he was opposed to the planned single European Union currency.

"We should not be part of a single European currency, but we've got to couch our views abour Europe in positive terms. We want to be in Europe but not run by Europe," he said in a reference the EU's drive for greater integration of the 15-nation bloc.

Whoever emerges as winner faces the formidable task of reuniting a Conservative Party divided by squabbles over Europe and reduced to half its size in the House of Commons by the Labour election landslide.
Although the leadership election is not expected before early summer, alliances have already begun to be declared.
Former education secretary Gillian Shephard, once mentioned as a possible leadership contender, announced she was backing Lilley.
